title: Lesson 24: Intellectual Property: Your Data, Your Outputs
description: Grounded in Lesson 24 of the AI Adoption series: the human authorship requirement and what it means for AI outputs, why a contract that says you own an output cannot manufacture a copyright, the data-use clause as the highest-value clause in an AI vendor agreement, the five stacked ownership questions, and the practical habits that keep a non-technical owner's data and most valuable outputs protected.

questions.question: According to Lesson 24, when does an AI-generated output get copyright protection in the United States?
options: Whenever a contract states that the customer owns the output
Whenever a vendor trains on the customer's data
Only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements of the output, such as through substantial editing, arrangement, or a human-authored work perceptible in the result
Whenever the output is generated by an enterprise AI tool
questions.explanation: The lesson is built on the human authorship requirement: copyright protects only material that is the product of human creativity, and a prompt alone does not make you the author. A work can be protected where a human determines sufficient expressive elements, for example by arranging, editing, or modifying the output so human expression is perceptible. A contract that says you own an output cannot create a copyright that the law does not recognize.

questions.question: In the worked example, why could the consulting firm not protect its flagship offer documents, and how did the data side fail?
options: The documents were too long to register, and the vendor refused to train on the data

The writers accepted most of the machine's expression and edited only lightly, so the outputs lacked protectable human authorship, and the firm had not read a data-use clause that allowed the vendor to use its data in aggregated or de-identified form for model training
The firm used a free tool, and free tools never hold copyright
The documents were all generated by a contractor rather than an employee
questions.explanation: Because the writers pasted most of the machine's expression and edited only lightly, the traditional elements of expression were determined by the AI, not the writers, so the outputs were largely unprotectable. On the data side, the firm signed a standard self-serve agreement without reading a data-use clause that let the vendor use customer data, inputs, outputs, and usage information in aggregated or de-identified form to improve models, putting confidential strategy and pricing into training.

questions.question: Which practice does Lesson 24 recommend for a non-technical owner to protect the organization's data and outputs?
options: Assume enterprise tools never train on data, and paste AI output unchanged to save time
Register every AI output as-is with the copyright office without disclosing AI use

Find and verify the data-use clause before routing sensitive data through a tool, classify confidential data by the color rule, require real human authorship for load-bearing outputs, assign rights from contractors in writing, and keep a record of the human contribution
Avoid using AI for any content a customer could see
questions.explanation: The lesson's practical moves are: find the data-use clause before you sign and confirm in writing that the vendor does not train without consent, route sensitive data using the red, yellow, green color rule, decide which outputs are load-bearing and require genuine human authorship for those, tell employees the difference between pasted output and authored work, assign contractor rights in writing, and preserve drafts that show the human contribution. Verification matters because the protections vary by vendor and must be checked in the actual contract, not assumed from marketing.
